title: From One Agent to Many
subtitle: Add specialists when their boundaries solve a demonstrated limitation
summary: Pip adds four specialist agents to the museum desk and visitors wait longer. Splitting work can improve focus, but creates interfaces, messages, and partial failures. Pip keeps specialists only where their boundaries justify the extra calls and coordination.

concepts.title: Single-agent fit
concepts.body: Pip’s meeting guide has three tools and a short history. One context holds the task comfortably. A single agent minimizes latency, resource use, and coordination overhead when responsibilities remain manageable. Pip measures a real limitation before recruiting another agent.

concepts.title: Specialization
concepts.body: Pip separates exhibition stock analysis from supplier comparison. Specialists focus on different roles or capabilities. Their structured results need interfaces and handoffs before a coordinator can combine a recommendation. Pip tests those boundaries as carefully as each specialist.

concepts.title: Communication patterns
concepts.body: Pip lets two specialists check independent suppliers in parallel. Delivery estimates wait for the supplier choice they depend on. Sequential messages, parallel work, coordinators, and shared state distribute context differently. Pip weighs latency, consistency, and failure propagation before choosing the communication pattern.

concepts.title: Coordination cost
concepts.body: Pip’s four-agent desk matches one agent’s quality but misses the response target. Extra agents add model calls, routing, synchronization, debugging, and operational expense. Pip removes the split that clarifies no useful boundary. Specialization must pay for its coordination, not merely look sophisticated.

misconceptions.claim: Single-agent fit is provided automatically by a more capable model.
misconceptions.correction: One agent is often suitable when tasks are modest, tools are manageable, and one context can hold the work. It minimizes latency, resource use, and coordination overhead.

misconceptions.claim: Specialization removes the need for evaluation or human judgment.
misconceptions.correction: Multiple agents divide work by role or capability, such as forecasting, procurement, or exception handling. Specialization can improve focus but creates interfaces and handoffs between agents. Evaluation and appropriate oversight remain necessary.

scenario.title: Supply-chain multiagent boundary
scenario.context: Forecasting, procurement, and exceptions need different tools; coordination time is limited.

options.label: Use specialists with explicit message contracts
options.benefit: Keeps roles focused and makes ownership visible.
options.cost: Calls and handoffs add latency and failure points.
options.consequence: A procurement agent rejects an incomplete forecast rather than guessing.

options.label: One generalist agent
options.cost: Tool overload makes selection and debugging difficult.
options.consequence: A single context mixes supplier and exception details.

scenario.debrief: Both choices can fit different constraints. The decision should state stakes, reversibility, evidence, and who owns correction.

quiz.question: Why begin with one agent when it can handle the workload?
options: One agent can never make a reasoning error.
Tools cannot be shared across agents.
It avoids unnecessary communication and coordination overhead.
quiz.explanation: A multiagent design should solve an actual limitation rather than add components by default.

quiz.question: Several specialists produce incompatible partial answers. What is missing?
options: Another copy of each conflicting answer.
quiz.explanation: Specialization requires a way to combine results and resolve disagreement.

quiz.question: What is a trade-off of separating specialist contexts?
options: Each agent gets focused context, but important information must cross boundaries.
All information is automatically available everywhere.
quiz.explanation: Context separation can improve focus while creating explicit handoff and consistency work.
